sections.b: These two chapters are the fullest teaching on the collection. Paul holds up the poor Macedonians who gave "beyond what they could" (8:3), asks Corinth to finish what it began a year earlier (8:10-11), and sets the rule of fairness: your surplus now meets their need, and their surplus may meet yours (8:13-14). The principle comes from Christ: "He was rich, and yet he became poor for your sake" (8:9). Paul sends Titus and two brothers chosen by the churches to handle the money so no one can find fault (8:16-23). Chapter 9 adds the farmer's rule and ends in thanks to God for a gift too great for words (9:6-15). He never calls it a 'collection' in these chapters: it is grace, sharing, service, blessing and generosity.

common: The collection was real relief for poor believers in Jerusalem and a sign of unity between Jewish and Gentile believers.
uncommon: Some read it as the 'offering of the nations' coming to Zion in the last days.

sections.b: Titus is Paul's go-between with Corinth. He carried the severe letter, waited for Paul's return, and came to Macedonia with good news: the church had repented and longed to see Paul (7:6-7, 13-15). Paul calls him "my partner and my fellow worker among you" (8:23). He had started the collection in Corinth a year earlier and was sent back to finish it (8:6, 16-17). Titus is never named in Acts. Paul says he was Greek and was not made to be circumcised in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1-5).

sections.h: The church and Paul's relations, chapters 6-9
sections.b: These chapters show a church in the middle of a repair. The Corinthians had been torn between loyalty to Paul and doubts raised against him; the severe letter and Titus's visit moved most of them back (7:5-16). Paul calls them his children (6:13) and pleads with them to open their hearts. He praises their eagerness, their faith and knowledge (8:7), and asks them to finish a collection they had begun. Behind the warm words stands a city of temples (6:16), patronage and status, in which the church was a mixed and not very wealthy group.

When asked for letters of recommendation (3:1), Paul answers with a catalog of hardships, virtues and paradoxes: he is called an impostor and is true, unknown and well known, dying and alive, poor and making many rich (6:4-10). The list matches the Acts of the Apostles at several points (beatings, prisons, riots) and 11:23-29 adds much more. It also shows how Paul understood apostleship: not strength displayed but weakness through which God works.

Paul lists nine troubles (pressures, beatings, prisons, riots, toil, sleepless nights, hunger), then answers each with a virtue and a paradox. The list borrows a form used by Greek and Roman teachers to show a wise person's endurance, but its aim is different: the troubles display God's power in weakness. The same pattern is in 4:7-12, 11:23-29 and 12:10.

Paul's teaching on giving: it is a grace, freely chosen, measured by what a person has (8:12), planned ahead (9:5), done cheerfully (9:7), and answered by God's supply for more giving (9:8-10). "God loves a glad giver" echoes the Greek of Proverbs 22:8a. "His righteousness remains forever" (Psalm 112:9) uses 'righteousness' in the sense the Jewish tradition gave it, generous giving to the poor.

Paul never asks the Corinthians for a tenth. In 8:12 and 9:7 he sets the manner of giving (willing, decided in the heart, by what a person has) and says nothing of a percentage. Churches that teach a tithe usually treat the tenth as a starting point and cite 9:7 for the spirit; churches that do not teach it point to this passage as the Christian rule. See the card on 2 Corinthians 9.

sections.h: Rich and poor in 2 Corinthians 8:9 and 9:8-11
sections.b: "He was rich, and yet he became poor for your sake" (8:9) is used in Christian teaching for the Incarnation and for generosity. It is also misused to promise money; in context it urges the comfortable to share with the poor. God supplies "all you need, and still have plenty for every good work" (9:8): a measure of enough, held for giving.

sections.h: The poor Macedonians and the poor in Jerusalem
sections.b: Both groups in the collection were poor. The Macedonians gave out of "deep poverty" (8:2); the Jerusalem saints were the beneficiaries (Romans 15:26). Paul says nothing about poverty being holy or shameful: it is a condition that calls for generosity, and a condition Christ took on (8:9).

Paul separates regret, grief in God's way and the grief of the world. His letter hurt the Corinthians; the hurt led to repentance, a turning that has no regret, and brought forth eagerness, a defense, anger, fear, longing, zeal and justice (7:11). The grief of the world only leads to death. The passage is the New Testament's clearest discussion of what makes sorrow turn into repentance.

After the promises of God's presence, welcome and fatherhood (6:16-18), Paul draws the conclusion: "let us wash ourselves clean of everything that soils flesh and spirit" and carry holiness through to the end (7:1). Holiness here is both a gift (the believers are God's temple) and a task. The churches differ on how far it can go in this life (see the card in chapter 7).

Paul's severe letter had asked the Corinthians to deal with a wrong done to him and to the church. They did so, and what they did is called a 'readiness to see justice done' (7:11). Paul did not write to punish for its own sake, but to test their loyalty and to see the matter put right. With 2:5-11 the passage shows discipline that ends in forgiveness.

sections.h: Idols and the temple of God, 2 Corinthians 6:14-18
sections.b: The question "How can God's temple agree with idols?" (6:16) draws a line between worship of the living God and the pagan temples of Corinth. It repeats the warning of 1 Corinthians 10:14-22 in the language of Israel's covenant and a second exodus: "get out from the middle of them" (2 Corinthians 6:17, from Isaiah 52:11).

sections.h: The church as God's temple, 2 Corinthians 6:16
sections.b: "It is we who are the temple of the living God" (6:16) joins 1 Corinthians 3:16-17 and 6:19, Ephesians 2:19-22 and 1 Peter 2:5 in saying that God's presence, once in the sanctuary, now lives among his people. Paul supports it with Leviticus 26:11-12 and Ezekiel 37:27, which promised God's dwelling with Israel.

"I will be their God, and they will be my people" is the covenant formula that runs through Leviticus 26:12, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 37:27. In 2 Corinthians 6:16-18 Paul joins it with a promise made to David's heir (2 Samuel 7:14) and applies the whole to a church of Gentiles and Jews: "you will be my sons and my daughters, says the Lord Almighty."
"What harmony is there between Christ and Beliar?" Beliar is a form of the Hebrew Belial, 'worthless.' This is the only time the New Testament uses the name, and it stands for Satan.

"Get out from the middle of them and keep yourselves apart" quotes Isaiah 52:11, the call to the exiles to leave Babylon, and "I will take you in" echoes Ezekiel 20:34, 41. The title of Webb's study places 6:14-7:1 in a 'second exodus' (return from exile) setting.

sections.h: The church in Jerusalem and the gift of the nations
sections.b: In 2 Corinthians 8-9 Jerusalem is the center that the Gentile churches serve with their gifts, a debt acknowledged in Romans 15:27. The gift was to be handled by delegates and brought to the "saints" there. Paul's last visit to Jerusalem was made to deliver it (Acts 24:17).

sections.h: 'He became poor for your sake', 2 Corinthians 8:9
sections.b: Paul gives Christ's self-giving as the pattern of Christian giving: he was rich and became poor so that we might be made rich. Readers disagree whether this refers to the Incarnation, to Jesus's earthly life or to his death; most take it to include his pre-existent glory.

The Greek charis appears ten times in these two chapters, for the gift and for the thanks it brings. Grace comes from God, passes through the Macedonians and the Corinthians to Jerusalem, and returns as thanks to God. The chapters end with thanks for a gift too great for words (9:15).

Paul gathers Israel's promises (a covenant of presence, a return, a father for David's heir) and says they are being kept in a church that includes Gentiles. Christian readers hear fulfillment and an enlargement of Israel's family; Jewish and 'Paul within Judaism' readers stress that he is speaking to non-Jews and does not take the promises from Israel.

Paul calls the two brothers "messengers of the churches" (apostoloi ekklesion), using 'apostle' in its plain sense of someone sent. He keeps the word for the office of those sent by Christ himself, a distinction that matters in chapters 10-13 where rivals claim a higher apostleship.

Paul quotes the words spoken to the Servant ("At a time of favor I listened to you") and adds "now is the day of salvation." He treats the Servant's day of rescue as arrived in Christ, with the church co-working in it (6:1).
